title: Minimax dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly in dimension d and horizon T, the information-theoretic minimax expected regret \(R*(d,T)\) for one-point adversarial bandit convex optimization with losses in \([0,1]\). Use the oblivious-adversary, exact-feedback model and worst-case normalized convex body defined below; logarithmic dependence is part of the requested rate.
why: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
status_note: The March 2026 primary book explicitly lists the minimax dimension dependence as open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching rate for the specified unrestricted one-point model. Recent smooth-loss and two-point results do not settle it.
review_note: Recovered the oblivious exact-observation model from the same author’s 2020 primary formulation; the imported proposal mentioned only one function value per round. Fixed loss range, affine domain normalization, expected minimax quantifiers and a fixed hindsight comparator. Kept the full joint rate question rather than choosing a conjectured exponent, and separated the book’s noisy and stochastic variants.

progress.text: A general information-theoretic upper bound \(O(d^{2.5} \sqrt{T} \log (T \operatorname{diam}(K)))\) is proved for the oblivious exact-feedback model.
The book’s Outlook retains the gap between dimension-linear lower bounds and higher-degree general upper bounds.
Budgeted-perturbation results concern smooth underlying losses, including in the unperturbed case.
The revised two-point strongly convex result has a different feedback and comparator model.

sentences: What is the optimal expected regret for adversarial convex losses when only one value is observed per round?
The learner competes with the best fixed point in hindsight over a known convex body.
The losses lie in \([0,1]\) and are chosen before the learner’s random actions, with no smoothness assumption.
General upper and lower bounds still have different polynomial dependence on dimension.
Two-point, strongly convex, smooth-loss and computational-efficiency results address different guarantees.

upgraded_from.title: Minimax dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization

definitions: Let \(d,T\ge 1\) be integers and \(B_{2}^{d}=\{x\in R^{d}:\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\le 1\}\). A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of \(R^{d}\) satisfying \(B_{2}^{d}\subseteq K\subseteq dB_{2}^{d}\); the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write \(F(K)\) for the Borel-measurable convex functions \(f:K\to [0,1]\), where convexity means \(f(\lambda x+(1- \lambda )y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1- \lambda )f(y)\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}\in F(K)\), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses \(X_{t}\in K\), incurs \(f_{t}(X_{t})\), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history \((X_{1},f_{1}(X_{1}),\ldots ,X_{t- 1},f_{t- 1}(X_{t- 1}))\). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define \(R_{K}(T)=\inf _{\pi} \sup _{f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}} E_{\pi}[\sum_{t} f_{t}(X_{t})- \inf _{x\in K}\sum_{t} f_{t}(x)]\), with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally \(R*(d,T)=\sup _{K} R_{K}(T)\), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function \(g(d,T)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) with a \(g(d,T)\le R*(d,T)\le b g(d,T)\) for all \(d,T\ge 1\). Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate \(g(d,T)\) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.

context_blocks.title: One value does not reveal a direction
context_blocks.text: On the interval \([- 1,1]\), the convex losses \(f(x)=(1+x)/2\) and \(h(x)=(1- x)/2\) both equal \(1/2\) at \(x=0\), but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

context_blocks.title: The benchmark is one fixed decision in hindsight
context_blocks.text: Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

context_blocks.title: Dimension remains a major gap
context_blocks.text: Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order \(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}\), apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as \(d\sqrt{T}\). The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in \([0,1]\); an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

context_blocks.title: Normalization and computational cost
context_blocks.text: Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

context_blocks.title: Which newer results change the assumptions
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.
